channel.title: Keith Dunstan
channel.description: The collected literary works of Keith Dunstan OAM

item.title: £5 for Most Mothers
item.description: The Senate passes the Fisher Government's Maternity Allowance in October 1912, a £5 payment for every white mother, wed or not, over the outrage of Senator St Ledger, who called it a sop to sin and adultery.

item.title: A Portrait or a Caricature?
item.description: Justice Roper rules in November 1944 that William Dobell's Archibald Prize-winning painting of fellow artist Joshua Smith is a portrait and not a caricature, ending a packed Equity Court case billed as the biggest legal smash hit since Ned Kelly.

item.title: Adventurer Lucky to be Alive
item.description: George Ernest Morrison, the 21-year-old Geelong walker the Age sponsored to cross New Guinea, reports from Cooktown in November 1883 that he was speared twice by local warriors and survived only because his companion Jack Lyons got him back to the coast.

item.title: A Poisoner Hanged
item.description: Martha Needle, who poisoned her whole family hoping to marry the carpenter Otto Juncken, is hanged at the Melbourne Gaol in October 1894, still protesting her innocence and calling the chaplain a liar on her way to the drop.

item.title: Alice Meets her Match in Veno
item.description: Sydney's champion Veno beats Victoria's mare Alice Hawthorne by three lengths in a 1000-sovereign match race at Flemington in October 1857, before up to 20,000 people, deflating a young colony desperate to prove itself superior to New South Wales.

item.title: Atomic Explosion at Monte Bello Islands
item.description: Britain explodes its first atomic bomb in the Monte Bello Islands off Western Australia in October 1952, rattling windows in Onslow, delighting a London press crowing about 'Our Bomb', and narrowly losing a race with the birth of the town's 'atomic baby'.

item.title: Black Fighter Exacts his Revenge
item.description: Jack Johnson takes the world heavyweight title from Tommy Burns at Hugh D. McIntosh's Rushcutters Bay stadium on Boxing Day 1908, the first world title fight between a black man and a white man, taunting 'poor little Tahmmy' for fourteen rounds until police stop the fight.

item.title: Australia's First Railway
item.description: The Melbourne and Hobson's Bay Railway opens in September 1854, its locally built 30-horsepower engine hauling Governor Charles Hotham and the colony's notables to Sandridge for a banquet in a zinc engine shed so noisy no one could hear the speeches.

item.title: Boxing Hero Wins World Title
item.description: Jimmy Carruthers becomes the first Australian-born world boxing champion in November 1952, knocking out bantamweight titleholder Vic Toweel in 139 seconds in Johannesburg, and tells the Argus by radio telephone that he never felt a punch.

item.title: Cable Trams Set Melbourne Agog
item.description: Melbourne's first cable trams start running from Spencer Street to the Hawthorn Bridge in November 1885, the reward for twenty years of lobbying by the American Francis Boardman Clapp against every State, city and municipal jealousy.

item.title: Bombala a Capital Idea
item.description: The House of Representatives picks Tumut and the Senate picks Bombala for the federal capital in October 1903, after members talk up their own electorates' climates, trees and women, and Billy Hughes dismisses Bombala's famous forests as mere shrubs.

item.title: Bushrangers on St Kilda Road
item.description: Five armed bushrangers hold up St Kilda Road for two and a half hours on an October afternoon in 1852, tying a score of travellers together in the wattle scrub within five miles of Melbourne, and the Argus blames Police Superintendent Evelyn Sturt.

item.title: Brawling and Looting in Police Strike
item.description: With some 800 Melbourne police on strike in November 1923, mobs take over the city block around Bourke and Swanston Streets, smashing 78 shop windows and looting jewellers and outfitters, while Premier Harry Lawson enrols 2000 special constables and refuses to take the strikers back.

item.title: Buckley Makes for the Bush
item.description: Giant convict bricklayer William Buckley escapes over Christmas 1803 from David Collins's short-lived settlement at Sullivan Bay on Port Phillip, and while his companions perish or come back starving, he lives with the Wathaurong people for 32 years.

item.title: Choosing a Federal Flag
item.description: The Commonwealth announces the winner of its 1901 flag competition, 32,823 entries strong and shared between five designers, while the Melbourne Herald sulks that its own striped design from 1900 was the better flag.

item.title: Burke and Wills Perish, but Archer Wins the Cup
item.description: In the week Melbourne learns that Burke and Wills have died, the Victoria Turf Club runs the first Melbourne Cup in November 1861, won by six lengths by the Sydney horse Archer after a fall that killed the mare Medora and broke a jockey's arm.

item.title: Conscripts will Not be Forced into Battle
item.description: Australians narrowly reject Billy Hughes's first conscription referendum in October 1916, carried by a resounding 'No' in New South Wales, after a bitter campaign of egg-pelted meetings, Nellie Melba's appeal for 'Yes' and a march of 10,000 'Hughesiliers' through Sydney.

item.title: Comet Flashes out of the Sky
item.description: C.W.A. Scott and Tom Campbell Black win the 1934 MacRobertson Centenary Air Race from London to Melbourne in their red DH.88 Comet, crossing the line at Flemington in just under three days after limping across the Timor Sea on one engine.

item.title: Collingwood Meets Melbourne and Supporters Go Beserk
item.description: A record 115,802 fans punch, claw and climb their way into the MCG for the 1956 Grand Final between Melbourne and Collingwood, forcing umpire Alan Nash to halt play while police clear spectators off the ground, before Melbourne thrashes Collingwood by 73 points.

item.title: Driving Out the Demon Drink
item.description: Melbourne's Federal Coffee Palace finally wins a liquor licence in November 1923, closing the noble era of temperance hotels that James Munro launched in the 1880s by ceremonially burning the Grand Hotel's licence at its opening banquet.

item.title: Electric Lamps Light up the Night
item.description: Spencer Street Station is lit by electric arc and incandescent lamps in November 1882, a demonstration by Sir Julius Vogel's Australasian Electric Light company that Railways Minister Thomas Bent toasts as the start of an illimitable future for electricity.

item.title: Emus V Army
item.description: The Emu War of 1932 sends Major G.P.W. Meredith and two Lewis guns to help wheat farmers at Campion in Western Australia, and after 10,000 rounds, a jammed gun and ridicule in the Senate, Defence Minister George Pearce can claim only 300 dead birds.

item.title: Fearful Affray at Eureka
item.description: Governor Sir Charles Hotham declares martial law after troopers storm the Eureka Stockade at Ballarat in December 1854, as the Age begs the diggers to lay down their arms and the Geelong Advertiser's man reports what looks less like an attack than a massacre.

item.title: Fighting Phylloxera
item.description: Victoria passes a law in December 1881 letting the Minister tear out every vine within 20 miles of Geelong Town Hall, a desperate bid to stop the phylloxera bug first found at Fyansford in 1877, which went on to ruin Rutherglen anyway.

item.title: For Nellie There's No Place Like Home
item.description: Nellie Melba gives her first homecoming concert at the Melbourne Town Hall in September 1902, after a royal progress south from Brisbane, a hard choice to leave her stricken father in hospital at Albury, and a reception the like of which no Australian had ever received.

item.title: Frank Hardy Charged with Libel
item.description: Frank Hardy is arrested for criminal libel in October 1950 over Power Without Glory, his barely disguised novel about John Wren, on a complaint that it accused Wren's wife Ellen of adultery, while copies sell under the counter for two pounds with a glossary of real names.

item.title: Free Banquet turns into Free-for-all
item.description: Melbourne's Citizens' Free Banquet for Prince Alfred, Duke of Edinburgh, in November 1867 descends into a drunken riot when the Duke fails to arrive and a ravenous crowd of 60,000 storms the tables, tears down the committee tent and drains a 500-gallon vat of wine.

item.title: Good Riddance to Sydney
item.description: News that the British Parliament has passed the Separation Bill reaches Port Phillip in November 1850, and Melbourne celebrates its freedom from New South Wales with beacons, a 21-gun salute, illuminated houses and shop transparencies mocking the 'Sydney robbers'.

item.title: Good-bye to the dear old Cables
item.description: Melbourne's last cable tram runs along Bourke Street in October 1940, quietly withdrawn by tramways chairman Hector Hercules Bell to foil souvenir hunters, ending 55 years of gripmen, kerosene lamps and the cry of 'Hold on for the curve please'.

item.title: Hargrave takes Flight
item.description: Lawrence Hargrave lifts himself 16 feet off the beach at Stanwell Park under a string of four box kites in November 1894, proving his curved-wing lifting surfaces while Sydney University's chancellor insists men will never fly.
